extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry and drama (poets, playwrights, critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetry—especially tragedy and epic—including what poetry essentially is, the parts and structure of tragedy, characteristics of good plots and characters, suitable language and musical/rhythmic means, and defenses against criticisms. Geared to creators and critics aiming to make or judge effective poetic drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (including epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyrambics, and airs) is essentially imitation — representing actions and characters by means of rhythm, harmony, and discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation differs in three particulars: the instruments it employs (rhythm, harmony, discourse), the objects imitated (better, worse, or like men), and the mode in which imitation is expressed (narration, enacted characters, mixed). Choose the appropriate combination to the genre and effect sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three means of poetic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is effected by rhythm (measured cadence/movement), harmony (music/melody), and discourse (speech/words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different arts use different combinations: music uses melody and rhythm; dance uses rhythm alone; epic uses discourse (verse or prose). Tragedy and comedy employ all three at times. Match means to genre (e.g., melody prominent in choruses; discourse and metre appropriate to spoken parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and end of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Tragedy is the imitation of a noble and perfect action, which is of a proper magnitude, expressed in agreeable language, producing a distinct pleasure, produced by action not narrative, and purifying the passions by means of fear and pity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The end (telos) of tragedy is to produce the wonderful and to excite and purge pity and fear (catharsis). Tragedy should enact events rather than merely recount them; select actions that provoke the proper emotional response through their structure and enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy (ordered importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is composed of six parts: (1) plot (story), (2) character (manner), (3) thought/sentiment, (4) diction/discourse (words), (5) melody, and (6) spectacle/scenery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the most important (the soul of tragedy); character and thought follow. Melody and spectacle contribute pleasure but are subordinate to plot and diction. In evaluation or composition, prioritize plot coherence and causal necessity before effects of staging or music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot and unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The story (plot, connection of actions) is of first importance; it must be a whole and complete action with a beginning, middle, and end — a single action so arranged that removal or alteration of any part changes the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere aggregation of episodes; ensure causal linkage and that each part is necessary. A well-constructed plot produces the emotions (pity/fear) by the internal development of action rather than by isolated incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole, completeness, and magnitude (proper length)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be entire (whole) and of a proper magnitude: neither too long nor too short — long enough to be effective but short enough to preserve unity and memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If too long, the beginning is forgotten before the end; if too short, the piece seems weak and loses unity by forced insertion of episodes. Greater length is acceptable only if perspicuity and unity are retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude over strict factual truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet need not confine himself to truth (what actually happened) but only to verisimilitude (what is probable or appears likely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry treats general types and principles rather than particular historical facts; choose incidents that seem plausible within the world of the poem. When accused of falsity, defend by pointing to probability, necessity, or conventional poetic usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs complex plot; peripeteia and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are simple (without reversal or recognition) or complex (containing peripeteia — reversal — and/or anagnorisis — recognition). The best plots often combine both, especially when recognition occurs at the same moment as reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for complex plots when you want powerful emotional effects; arrange reversals and recognitions to feel inevitable and to arise from the chain of events rather than contrivance. Avoid recognitions produced merely by contrived tokens when a chain-of-events solution is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred tragic protagonist (character type)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragic subject is a man who is neither eminent for virtue nor for wickedness, who falls from happiness to misery through some great error (hamartia) and not through an entirely wicked deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be of high standing so their fall matters, but not perfect or irredeemably evil — this engenders pity and fear. The error should be plausible and connected to character; avoid pure villainy or undeserved catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causing pity and fear through causal connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity should arise from the connection of events — the plot itself — so that mere narration without enactment would still produce those feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select events and causal relations that will generate pity and fear even when read; assemble incidents so the audience apprehends how the change of fortune follows from actions and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of effecting recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition can be produced by: (1) physical marks on the body, (2) causes invented by the poet, (3) excitation of recollection, (4) force of inference, and (5) chain of events; the latter (chain of events) is the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that emerge logically from events rather than arbitrary tokens or sudden contrivances; invent causes only when necessary and make them plausible within the world of the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character portrayal: useful, becoming, like, and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: When shaping characters the author must ensure the manner given is useful to the plot, becoming to the person, like (probable), and equal (consistent across the piece).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters’ actions and speech must suit their established habits and social position, be believable, and serve the action. Use the chain of motives; avoid actions that contradict previously established character without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of machinery and absence of purposeless action
rubrics_metrics.description: Machinery (deus ex machina or external devices) should be used only when relating circumstances outside the representation; no action must appear to be without an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implausible supernatural or arbitrary devices that break causal integrity. If machinery is introduced, make its necessity and relation to the story clear, or prefer to resolve within the human chain of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition process: outline then fill; ask 'why'
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should first draw a general outline of the story (plot) and then fill it up; frequently question why characters do what they do to avoid errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep checking motives and causal relations during composition; this practice reduces inconsistencies. Similarly, actors should adapt gesture and voice to the passion intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of tragedy by quantity and chorus function
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy’s parts by quantity are prologue, episode, exode, and chorus (which has parodos and stasimon); the chorus is a part of the company of performers and its songs ought always to have reference to the subject of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus integrally: their parodos (first speech) and stasima (choral odes) should comment on, enrich, and harmonize with the plot rather than distract. The chorus helps produce pleasure, chiefly by melody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and rhetorical excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence of discourse is that it be perspicuous without being mean; proper application of metaphor is most important; use words fittingly (proper nouns, foreign words, invented words, extended/diminished forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermix noun types properly; avoid overuse of any one form; employ metaphors judiciously. Tailor diction to metre and genre (double words for dithyrambics, foreign words for heroic, metaphor for iambic verse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of speech and action (fit to person/time/place/end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether anything said or done is becoming should be judged not only by the thing itself but by who says/does it, to whom, at what time, in what manner, and for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate single passages in their full context: a speech that seems improper may be appropriate given character, situation, and aim. Consider whether a greater good or avoidance of greater evil justifies an action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense against criticisms and use of poetic licence
rubrics_metrics.description: When critics call incidents impossible or untrue, the poet may defend them by showing the credible impossible is preferable to the possible incredible, by appealing to poetic aims, or to common report and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use probability, necessity, and exemplary perfection as defenses. Don’t include improbable elements unless they are necessary to the plot’s end; avoid gratuitous unreasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of incidents for epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry should represent a whole and perfect action with a beginning, middle, and end (like tragedy) but differs in length and measure; epic can include episodes and shift scene more freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hexameter (heroic) for epic; aim for the wonderful and for verisimilitude that maintains interest. Prefer incidents that, while perhaps impossible, retain plausibility. Epic language should be highly polished especially when not carrying manner or sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre–form matching (meter, rhythm, and voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres suit different metres, rhythms, and word-types: heroic (hexameter) fits epic, iambic verse suits iambic/tragicomedy modes, and certain noun/word-types pair naturally with particular genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match metre and diction to the genre: double words with dithyrambics, foreign words with heroic, metaphor with iambic. Avoid mixing incompatible metres gratuitously; mixed rhapsodies lose poet status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faults to avoid: overreaching and wrong subject choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of faults exist for the poet: attempting to imitate things beyond the art’s stretch (overreaching), and improperly choosing subject matter within reach (wrong choice by accident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t attempt subjects that require technical knowledge or skill beyond the poet’s competence unless absolutely necessary. If choosing within reach, select well; accidental poor choice is still blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenery and spectacle as subsidiary
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery/spectacle (opsis) contributes to pleasure but is of the least artistic importance among the parts of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on spectacle to enhance but not substitute for plot and characterization. Excessive dependence on visual effects signals weakness in the poetic art rather than strength.
